title: How should a caption distinguish a material close-up from an installation photograph?
description: State whether the image is a close-up, a whole-object view, a concept scene or a verified installation photograph.

sections.heading: How should a caption distinguish a material close-up from an installation photograph?
paragraphs: State whether the image is a close-up, a whole-object view, a concept scene or a verified installation photograph. Explain what the detail is being used to show and link it to the wider source where available. Do not add a client, location or completion claim merely because the image looks realistic or has a suggestive filename.

title: How are design visualizations labelled?
description: Design visualizations carry a disclosure indicating that they are illustrative.

sections.heading: How are design visualizations labelled?
paragraphs: Design visualizations carry a disclosure indicating that they are illustrative. Concept Portfolio entries also state that they are not completed customer projects. Read that label alongside the image and caption. Realistic rendering does not establish a real installation, verified material property or exact finished appearance, and a reference image is not necessarily a rendering of the described concept.

title: What qualifies as a genuine portfolio project?
description: A genuine project needs a distinct source identity, factual brief and response, project-specific evidence, permitted attribution and publication approval.

sections.heading: What qualifies as a genuine portfolio project?
paragraphs: A genuine project needs a distinct source identity, factual brief and response, project-specific evidence, permitted attribution and publication approval. Several images of one project remain one record. The labelled concept studies are educational proposals and do not count as completed commissions. Missing evidence cannot be replaced by an invented customer, location or completion date.

title: Can a room image alone prove an installation?

sections.heading: Can a room image alone prove an installation?
paragraphs: No. A room image may be a visualization, a reference or an unrelated photograph. A real installation claim needs source evidence tied to the actual project and permission for the proposed public use. Photorealism and filenames are not enough. When the source is a concept, the caption and surrounding story must keep that classification clear.

title: Why might a project omit a customer's name or location?
description: Public attribution depends on the permission granted for that story and its images.

sections.heading: Why might a project omit a customer's name or location?
paragraphs: Public attribution depends on the permission granted for that story and its images. A customer may permit an object to be shown while keeping their name, location or personal history private. The public wording should follow the actual allowed scope. Omitted details should remain omitted rather than being replaced with invented identifying information.

title: Can a testimonial be published without attribution permission?
description: Genuine feedback publication requires a recorded source, permission for the intended use and approved public attribution.

sections.heading: Can a testimonial be published without attribution permission?
paragraphs: Genuine feedback publication requires a recorded source, permission for the intended use and approved public attribution. Do not invent an anonymous identity or assume private feedback can be published. The exact permission may allow a limited attribution, but it must be recorded. Fictional samples are separately labelled and are not customer feedback or evidence of consent.

title: Do translated quotes count as different reviews?

sections.heading: Do translated quotes count as different reviews?
paragraphs: No. A translated quote remains the same underlying feedback record. Multiple languages, placements or images do not create additional testimonials. Preserve the original meaning and permitted attribution, and keep language review separate from source and consent approval. A machine-assisted translation is not evidence that a native reader has reviewed the published wording.

title: Can several photographs represent one project?

sections.heading: Can several photographs represent one project?
paragraphs: Yes. Several views can explain one project or concept, such as an overview and a detail. They should remain tied to the same source identity where appropriate. More photographs do not mean more completed projects. Label reference images that merely inform a concept so they are not mistaken for documentation of its construction or installation.

title: Where can I find related project information?
description: Use related links on the entry or browse the relevant Portfolio or Journal topic.

sections.heading: Where can I find related project information?
paragraphs: Use related links on the entry or browse the relevant Portfolio or Journal topic. Check the classification and purpose of each linked record: a concept study, guidance article and genuine project story answer different questions. A related link does not prove the records describe the same customer or commission. Keep useful references for the discussion.

title: How do I ask about the source of a pictured piece?
description: Identify the page and image, then ask the atelier what source or classification applies.

sections.heading: How do I ask about the source of a pictured piece?
paragraphs: Identify the page and image, then ask the atelier what source or classification applies. Include the visible title or reference so the question is precise. Do not infer a customer, location, material identity or available product from the image alone. Captions and disclosures should state known information; unresolved provenance remains a question.
